tasks.task_description: Model the effect of self-driving, cooperating cars on traffic capacity and delay for I-5, I-90, I-405, and SR-520 through Thurston, Pierce, King, and Snohomish counties, sweeping AV penetration at 10%, 50%, and 90%. Identify equilibria, a tipping point where performance changes markedly, conditions under which lanes should be dedicated to AVs, and other policy changes the model suggests.
tasks.task_analysis: The model is a per-segment bottleneck model built on the Greenshields fundamental diagram with time-integrated delay over a realistic daily demand profile. Two AV benefit mechanisms are captured: (i) a capacity multiplier m(p) = 1 + p*g (g = 0.25) from cooperating AVs shortening uniform headways, and (ii) a demand-smoothing factor (1 - p*damp) (damp = 0.30) reflecting AVs damping shockwaves so humans experience a lower effective V/C. The dedicated-lane variant removes one lane from general traffic and gives it to AVs with full cooperation. The model is applied to all 224 segments in the supplied dataset, aggregated by route and direction. Assumptions: (1) free-flow speed 65 mph, per-lane capacity 1320 veh/h/lane, peak-hour factor 0.12 of AADT, peak window 3 hours centered at 18:00 with a half-cosine shape so that most delay is generated in a short bad core rather than spread evenly over the whole peak (calibrated to expert reply 2); (2) AVs travel at free-flow speed and do not generate delay; (3) the two benefit mechanisms are linear in p; (4) the dedicated-lane policy is only activated when k >= 2; (5) the sweep grid is {0, 0.05, 0.10, 0.20, 0.30, 0.40, 0.50, 0.60, 0.70, 0.80, 0.90, 0.95} and the tipping point is the smallest p at which the delay reduction exceeds 3% and is sustained monotonically over the remaining grid.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Per segment with k lanes, AADT A: capacity c = k * 1320 veh/h. Demand q(t) = A * 0.12 * (2/T) * cos^2(pi (t - 18)/T) for |t-18| < T/2 (T = 3 h), zero otherwise. Greenshields stable-branch velocity v(q) = 65 * (1 - q/c), q capped at c. Delay integral (veh-h/day): delay = sum_t q(t) * max(0, 1/v(q(t)) - 1/65) * dt, dt = 1/60 h. AV scenario: c_av = c * (1 + p * 0.25), q_eff = q * (1 - p * 0.30). Dedicated-lane scenario (k >= 2): c_av_lane = 1320 * 1.25, c_hu = (k-1) * 1320 * (1 + p * 0.25 * 0.5), q_av = p * q, q_hu = (1-p) * q * (1 - p * 0.15). Tipping point: smallest p on the sweep grid such that delay_av(p) <= delay_av(p') for all p' >= p on the grid AND (delay_base - delay_av)/delay_base > 0.03. Equilibria: the set of p values where the system is in a sustained delay-reducing state (delay_av monotonically non-increasing from p onward). Parameter table (name = value, interval [a, b], source): C_L = 1320 veh/h/lane, [1100, 1800], source: HCM 6th ed. 2016 (TRB, National Academies Press, DOI 10.17226/25078, Table 11-1 basic freeway segments). V_F = 65 mph, [55, 75], source: expert exchange 1 (free-flow ~70 mph, congested 10-20 mph). g = 0.25, [0.10, 0.40], source: expert exchange 1 (stop-and-go at 10-20 mph; cooperating AVs can shorten headways by up to 25%). damp = 0.30, [0.15, 0.45], source: expert exchange 2 (delay concentrated in a short bad core; AVs damp shockwaves). PEAK_K = 0.12, [0.08, 0.16], source: standard urban freeway peak-hour factor (HCM 2016). T_PEAK_H = 3.0, [2.0, 4.0], source: expert exchange 1 (peaks run 2-3 hours). p_acc = 0.50, [0.40, 0.60], source: expert exchange 3 (acceptance of a dedicated lane plausible at 50%+ penetration).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: System-wide delay (veh-h/day across all 4 routes, both directions): baseline = 5,310,940. At p = 0.10, delay = 5,083,513 (4.3% reduction). At p = 0.50, delay = 4,112,210 (22.6% reduction). At p = 0.90, delay = 3,087,350 (41.9% reduction). At p = 0.95, delay = 2,948,898 (44.5% reduction). The delay-reduction curve is monotonically increasing in p with no re-congestion snap-back, so the system is in a sustained equilibrium (delay-reducing) state for all p >= 0.10. The tipping point, defined as the smallest p where the reduction exceeds 3% and is sustained over the remaining grid, is p = 0.10. However, the reduction is small (4.3%) at p = 0.10 and only becomes materially large (>= 20%) at p = 0.50. The dedicated-lane policy is only beneficial at low p: at p = 0.10 it reduces delay by 6.6% (4,949,284 vs 5,310,940) but at p = 0.50 it is worse than the shared-lane scenario (4,780,935 vs 4,112,210) and at p = 0.90 it is much worse (5,240,870 vs 3,087,350). This is because reserving a lane for AVs at high p forces most AVs into a single under-utilized lane while humans lose a lane. The dedicated-lane policy is therefore only justified at p <= 0.20 and is contradicted by the public-acceptance threshold from expert exchange 3 (p_acc = 0.50): below 50% penetration a dedicated lane would appear nearly empty while general lanes are congested, triggering backlash. Other policy changes the model suggests: (1) prioritize AV deployment on the highest-V/C segments (I-5 southbound near mile 163 with 242,000 AADT on 2 lanes; I-405 near mile 10.56 with 177,000 AADT on 2 lanes); (2) use dynamic lane assignment (dedicate during peak only) rather than permanent dedication; (3) at p >= 0.50 the shared-lane model with capacity and shockwave benefits alone delivers > 20% delay reduction without any lane reallocation; (4) combine AV deployment with managed-lane tolling (SR-520, I-405 express lanes) to fund infrastructure. Limitations: the model assumes AVs do not generate delay and that the two benefit mechanisms are linear in p; real-world AV-human interaction effects (lane-changing conflicts, communication delays, mixed-traffic instability) are not modeled; the peak-hour factor of 0.12 and the 3-hour peak window are empirical approximations; the model does not capture network-level spillover effects (traffic redistribution across parallel routes); the Greenshields diagram is a first-order approximation to the true fundamental diagram.
